Q: How to check if Make has seen stale include directives during parsing? A:

But how do I tell during the first parse that I have stale includes, so that I can avoid executing $(info ...)?

You don't, and you've very nearly explained why yourself. You would need to make the determination during the parse to avoid executing the $(info) call, which is itself performed during the parse. But make cannot and does not attempt to determine whether any file is out of date until after it has fully parsed the makefile.

With GNU make, you can determine whether the current parse is the first via the MAKE_RESTARTS variable, but there is no mechanism for determining during parsing whether there will be another parse.

It's unclear whether your focus here is on emitting the message or more generally on detecting during parsing whether there will be a restart. If the latter then you're out of luck. If the former, however, you could do it by using a rule to emit the message. Make most other rules depend on the target of the message rule, which can be phony, and then the message will not be emitted until after make determines that there is no need for any more restarts.

Q: GetIsNetworkAvailable() behaves differently depending on .NET version A:

Let me talk about the reason first. This PR resulted in the return of some NDIS interfaces by the NetworkInterface.GetAllNetworkInterfaces method, some of them are not actually connected, but their OperationalStatus is always Up.

So this is only a problem on Windows, I can think 5 ways to solve it:

  1. Use the Windows API GetAdaptersAddresses, but do not pass the GAA_FLAG_INCLUDE_ALL_INTERFACES flag, in order to get the same result as .NET8.

  2. Further filtering of the existing results returned by GetAllNetworkInterfaces. You can check whether the interface has ipv4 support, a physical address, gateway, or unicast address:

    bool isNetworkReallyAvailable = NetworkInterface
     .GetAllNetworkInterfaces()
     .Any(ni =>
          ni.OperationalStatus == OperationalStatus.Up &&
          ni.NetworkInterfaceType != NetworkInterfaceType.Loopback &&
          ni.NetworkInterfaceType != NetworkInterfaceType.Tunnel &&
          // Choose one
          (ni.Supports(NetworkInterfaceComponent.IPv4) ||
          ni.GetPhysicalAddress().Equals(PhysicalAddress.None) ||
          ni.GetIPProperties().GatewayAddresses.Count > 0 ||
          ni.GetIPProperties().UnicastAddresses.Count > 0)
     );

  3. You can remove those interfaces: https://superuser.com/questions/1257859/remove-an-unused-hidden-network-connection-so-that-an-existing-name-can-be-reuse

  4. Go back to .NET8, fire an issue on github, and wait for a later version to fix it.

  5. Consider using other methods, such as this, this, and this.

Q: What response should I return when my get response is empty A:

What response should I return when my get response is empty

Rules first: you should return a 200 when your resource (the thing identified by your universal resource identifier) includes the current representation of the resource, and you should return 404 when your resource has no current representation (in which case the response body is a representation of an explanation for the error situation).

See RFC 9110 and Fielding's Dissertation for definitions of "resource" and "representation".

Neither REST nor HTTP attempt to answer "when does my resource not have a current representation?"

In other words, what RFC 9110 is doing is introducing some constraints on the semantics (meaning) of the messages we pass around, but not introducing any constraints on your implementation.

200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

null

Is a perfectly legal and legitimate response; the client asked for the current representation of the resource, you happen to have one, here it is.

200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{}

200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
"title": null,
"message": null
}

Both of these choices are also fine.

That said, you are also permitted to design your resources such that their representations are most convenient for whatever target audience you want. If the remote actor in your use case is an API client designed by people most comfortable with Rails conventions, or most comfortable with OpenAPI, or whatever, then you design your resource model with those additional constraints in mind, and choose the general purpose HTTP responses that best match.

REST and HTTP really don't care about the fashion of the day, which is part of the reason that they are still around / relevant after 25+ years.

204 No Content has a specific circumstance that it is designed for, and if it doesn't closely match what you are doing, you should probably avoid it

The 204 response allows a server to indicate that the action has been successfully applied to the target resource, while implying that the user agent does not need to traverse away from its current "document view" (if any).

See also the language of 205 Reset Content.

204 is not best understood as a special case that you are supposed to use when the current representation of the resource is 0 bytes long. For that case, you should strongly prefer to send a 200 response with Content-Length: 0.

Furthermore, if your Content-Type is application/json, then your representation is never 0 bytes long (the shortest semantically valid json document is a number with exactly 1 digit). See RFC 8259.

Q: Data visualization with clear bars on a histogram? A:

I often have this situation and I usually just plot the histograms as curves using numpy:

Toy setup:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


n_sets = 7
n_samples = 10**4

scales = np.linspace(0.8, 1.2, n_sets)
data = np.random.rand(n_sets, n_samples)**scales[:,None]

bins = np.linspace(0,1,10)

Messy histograms with plt.hist:

plt.figure(1).clf()
for d in data:
    plt.hist(d, bins, alpha=0.3)

Now using np.histogram and regular plt.plot :

plt.figure(2).clf()
for d in data:
    counts, bins = np.histogram(d, bins)
    plt.plot(bins[:-1], counts)
plt.ylim(0, plt.ylim()[1])

(and if you need convincing that plt.hist and np.histogram do compute the same thing, you can retreive the exact same result by replacing plt.plot(bins_for_plot, counts) with plt.bar(bins_for_plot, counts, bar_width, alpha=0.3) and bar_width = bins_for_plot[1] - bins_for_plot[0], or you can check directly that all(all(x == y) for x,y in zip(plt.hist(d, bins), np.histogram(d, bins))))

Q: Set-ExecutionPolicy gloablly for a specific script A:

No.

As documented, there is no concept of setting the EP at the script level.

You have to do it as you have already shown...

powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Script\From\Internet.ps1

... which btw is not at the script level (since there is no such thing), you are the default process level.

You can add it, the EP, to your profile(s)...

  • Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1
  • Microsoft.PowerShellISE_profile.ps1
  • Microsoft.VSCode_profile.ps1

... but that applies to any PowerShell instance you start.

Again, as documented, there are only 5 options (file/script is not one of them):

  1. MachinePolicy
  2. UserPolicy
  3. Process
  4. CurrentUser
  5. LocalMachine

Your only option to get close to what you are after is to create a custom shortcut on your desktop using the command you have already shown and pin that to wherever you need it.

The only real reason to change the EP is if the Machine EP is more restrictive (Restricted or AllSigned) enforce via GPO and you need to work outside that.
